Later, James and Stein (1961) established the complete dominance of (4.20) over X, and (4.20) remains the basic underlying form of almost all improved estimators. In particular, the appearance of the squared term in the shrinkage factor is essential for optimality (Brown 1971; Berger 1976a; Berger 1985, Section 8.9.4). 

Since Stein (1956b) and James and Stein (1961), the proof of domination of the estimator (4.20) over the maximum likelihood estimator, X, has undergone many modifications and updates. More recent proofs are based on the representation of Corollary 4.7.2 and can be made to apply to cases other than the normal. We defer treatment of this topic until Section 5.6. At present, we only make some remarks about the estimator (4.20) and the following modifications due to James and Stein (1961). Let 

$$
\delta_ {i} = \mu_ {i} + \left(1 - \frac {r - 2}{| \mathbf {x} - \mu | ^ {2}}\right) (x _ {i} - \mu_ {i})\tag{4.21}
$$

where $\pmb{\mu} = (\mu_1, \dots, \mu_r)$ are given numbers and 

$$
\left| \mathbf {x} - \boldsymbol {\mu} \right| = \left[ \Sigma (x _ {i} - \mu_ {i}) ^ {2} \right] ^ {1 / 2}.\tag{4.22}
$$

A motivation for the general structure of the estimator (4.21) can be obtained by using arguments similar to the empirical Bayes arguments in Examples 4.7.7 and 4.7.8 (see also Problems 4.7.6 and 4.7.7). Suppose, a priori, it was thought likely, though not certain, that $\theta_{i} = \mu_{i}$ ( $i = 1, \ldots, r$ ). Then, it might be reasonable first to test 

$$
H: \theta_ {1} = \mu_ {1}, \ldots , \theta_ {r} = \mu_ {r}
$$

and to estimate $\pmb{\theta}$ by $\pmb{\mu}$ when $H$ is accepted and by $\mathbf{X}$ otherwise. The best acceptance region has the form $|\mathbf{x} - \pmb{\mu}| \leq C$ so that the estimator becomes 

$$
\delta = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \boldsymbol {\mu} & \text { if } | \mathbf {x} - \boldsymbol {\mu} | \leq C \\ \mathbf {x} & \text { if } | \mathbf {x} - \boldsymbol {\mu} | > C. \end{array} \right.\tag{4.23}
$$

A smoother approach is provided by an estimator with components of the form 

$$
\delta_ {i} = \psi (| \mathbf {x} - \pmb {\mu} |) x _ {i} + [ 1 - \psi (| \mathbf {x} - \pmb {\mu} |) ] \mu_ {i}\tag{4.24}
$$

where $\psi$ , instead of being two-valued as in (4.23), is a function increasing continuously with $\psi(0)=0$ to $\psi(\infty)=1$ . The estimator (4.21) is of the form (4.24) (although with $\psi(0)=-\infty$ ), but the argument given above provides no explanation of the particular choice for $\psi$ . We note, however, that many hierarchical Bayes estimators (such as given in Example 5.2) will result in estimators of this form. We will return to this question in Section 5.6. 

For the case of unknown $\sigma$ , the estimator corresponding to (4.23) has been investigated by Sclove, Morris, and Radhakrishnan (1972). They show that it does not provide a uniform improvement over X and that its risk is uniformly greater than that of the corresponding James-Stein estimator. Although these so-called pretest estimators tend not to be optimal, they have been the subject of considerable research (see, for example, Sen and Saleh 1985, 1987). 

Unlike X, the estimator $\delta$ is, of course, biased. An aspect that in some circumstances is disconcerting is the fact that the estimator of $\theta_{i}$ depends not only on $X_{i}$ but also on the other (independent) X's. Do we save enough in risk to make up for these drawbacks? To answer this, we take a closer look at the risk function. 

Under the loss (4.17), it will be shown in Theorem 5.1 that the risk function of the estimator (4.21) can be written as 

$$
R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) = 1 - \frac {r - 2}{r} E _ {\theta} \left(\frac {r - 2}{| \mathbf {X} - \boldsymbol {\mu} | ^ {2}}\right).\tag{4.25}
$$

Thus, $\delta$ has uniformly smaller risk than the constant estimator X when $r \geq 3$ , and, in particular, $\delta$ is then minimax by Example 4.6. More detailed information can be obtained from the fact that $|X - \mu|^{2}$ has a noncentral $\chi^{2}$ -distribution with noncentrality parameter $\lambda = \Sigma(\theta_{i} - \mu_{i})^{2}$ and that, therefore, the risk function (4.25) is an increasing function of $\lambda$ . (See TSH2 Chapter 3, Lemma 2 and Chapter 7, Problem 4 for details). The risk function tends to 1 as $\lambda \to \infty$ , and takes on its minimum value at $\lambda = 0$ . For this value, $|X - \mu|^{2}$ has a $\chi^{2}$ -distribution with r degrees of freedom, and it follows from Example 2.1 that (Problem 4.7) 

$$
E \left(\frac {1}{| \mathbf {X} - \boldsymbol {\mu} | ^ {2}}\right) = \frac {1}{r - 2}
$$

and hence $R(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \delta) = 2/r$ . Particularly for large values of r, the savings over the risk of X (which is equal to 1 for all $\theta$ ) can therefore be substantial. (See Bondar 1987 for further discussion.) 

We thus have the surprising result that X is not only inadmissible when $r \geq 3$ but that even substantial risk savings are possible. This is the case not only for squared error loss but also for a wide variety of loss functions which in a suitable way combine the losses resulting from the r component problems. In particular, Brown (1966, Theorem 3.1.1) proves that X is inadmissible for $r \geq 3$ when $L(\boldsymbol{\theta}, d) = \rho(d - \boldsymbol{\theta})$ , where $\rho$ is a convex function satisfying, in addition to some mild conditions, the requirement that the $r \times r$ matrix R with the $(i, j)$ th element 

$$
E _ {0} \left[ X _ {i} \frac {\partial}{\partial X _ {j}} \rho (\mathbf {X}) \right]\tag{4.26}
$$

is nonsingular. Here, the derivative in (4.26) is replaced by zero whenever it does 

not exist. 

Example 4.7 A variety of loss functions. Consider the following loss functions $\rho_{1},\ldots ,\rho_{4}$ : 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \rho_ {1} (\mathbf {t}) = \Sigma v _ {i} t _ {i} ^ {2} \qquad (\text { all   } v _ {i} > 0); \\ \rho_ {2} (\mathbf {t}) = \max _ {i} t _ {i} ^ {2}; \\ \rho_ {3} (\mathbf {t}) = t _ {1} ^ {2}, \\ \rho_ {4} (\mathbf {t}) = \left(\frac {1}{r} \Sigma t _ {i}\right) ^ {2}. \end{array}
$$

All four are convex, and $\mathcal{R}$ is nonsingular for $\rho_{1}$ and $\rho_{2}$ but singular for $\rho_{3}$ and $\rho_{4}$ (Problem 4.8). For $r \geq 3$ , it follows from Brown's theorem that $\mathbf{X}$ is inadmissible for $\rho_{1}$ and $\rho_{2}$ . On the other hand, it is admissible for $\rho_{3}$ and $\rho_{4}$ (Problem 4.10). 

Other ways in which the admissibility of $\mathbf{X}$ depends on the loss function are indicated by the following example (Brown, 1980b) in which $L(\pmb{\theta},d)$ is not of the form $\rho(d - \pmb{\theta})$ . 

Example 4.8 Admissibility of X. Let $X_{i}$ ( $i = 1, \ldots, r$ ) be independently distributed as $N(\theta_{i}, 1)$ and consider the estimation of $\theta$ with loss function 

$$
L (\pmb {\theta}, d) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} \frac {v (\theta_ {i})}{\Sigma v (\theta_ {j})} (\theta_ {i} - d _ {i}) ^ {2}.\tag{4.27}
$$

Then the following results hold: 

(i) When $v(t) = e^{kt}$ ( $k \neq 0$ ), $\mathbf{X}$ is inadmissible if and only if $r \geq 2$ . 

(ii) When $v(t) = (1 + t^2)^{k/2}$ , 

(a) $\mathbf{X}$ is admissible for $k < 1$ , $1 \leq r < (2 - k) / (1 - k)$ and for $k \geq 1$ , all $r$ ; 

(b) $\mathbf{X}$ is inadmissible for $k < 1, r > (2 - k) / (1 - k)$ . 

Parts (i) and (ii(b)) will not be proved here. For the proof of (ii(a)), see Problem 4.11. 

In the formulations considered so far, the loss function in some way combines the losses resulting from the different component problems. Suppose, however, that the problems of estimating $\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{r}$ are quite unrelated and that it is important to control the error on each of them. It might then be of interest to minimize 

$$
\max _ {i} \left[ \sup _ {\theta_ {i}} E (\delta_ {i} - \theta_ {i}) ^ {2} \right].\tag{4.28}
$$

It is easy to see that X is the unique estimator minimizing (4.28) and is admissible from this point of view. This follows from the fact that $X_{i}$ is the unique estimator for which 

$$
\sup _ {\theta_ {i}} E (\delta_ {i} - \theta_ {i}) ^ {2} \leq 1.
$$

[On the other hand, it follows from Example 4.7 that $\mathbf{X}$ is inadmissible for $r \geq 3$ when $L(\pmb{\theta}, d) = \max_{i} (d_{i} - \theta_{i})^{2}$ .] 

The performance measure (4.28) is not a risk function in the sense defined in Chapter 1 because it is not the expected value of some loss but the maximum of a number of such expectations. An interesting way of looking at such a criterion was proposed by Brown (1975) [see also Bock 1975, Shinozaki 1980, 1984]. Brown considers a family L of loss functions L, with the thought that it is not clear which of these loss functions will be most appropriate. (It may not be clear how the data will be used, or they may be destined for multiple uses. In this connection, see also Rao 1977.) If 

$$
R _ {L} (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) = E _ {\theta} L [ \boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta (\mathbf {X}) ],\tag{4.29}
$$

Brown defines $\delta$ to be admissible with respect to the class $\mathcal{L}$ if there exists no $\delta'$ such that 

$$
R _ {L} (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta^ {\prime}) \leq R _ {L} (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) \quad \text { for   all } \quad L \in \mathcal {L} \text {   and   all   } \boldsymbol {\theta}
$$

with strict inequality holding for at least one $L = L_0$ and $\pmb{\theta} = \pmb{\theta}_0$ . 

The argument following (4.28) shows that X is admissible when L contains the r loss functions $L_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, d) = (d_{i} - \theta_{i})^{2}$ , $i = 1, \ldots, r$ , and hence, in particular, when L is the class of all loss functions 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} c _ {i} (\delta_ {i} - \theta_ {i}) ^ {2}, \quad 0 \leq c _ {i} <   \infty .\tag{4.30}
$$

On the other hand, Brown shows that if the ratios of the weights $c_{i}$ to each other are bounded, 

$$
c _ {i} / c _ {j} <   K, \quad i, j = 1, \dots , r,\tag{4.31}
$$

then no matter how large K, the estimator X is inadmissible with respect to the class L of loss functions (4.30) satisfying (4.31). Similar results persist in even more general settings, such as when L is not restricted to squared error loss. See Hwang 1985, Brown and Hwang 1989, and Problem 4.14. 

The above considerations make it clear that the choice between X and competitors such as $(4.21)$ must depend on the circumstances. (In this connection, see also Robinson 1979a, 1979b). A more detailed discussion of some of these issues will be given in the next section. 

## 5 Shrinkage Estimators in the Normal Case

The simultaneous consideration of a number of similar estimation problems involving independent variables and parameters $(X_{i}, \theta_{i})$ often occurs in repetitive situations in which it may be reasonable to view the $\theta$ 's themselves as random variables. This leads to the Bayesian approach of Examples 4.7.1, 4.7.7, and 4.7.8. In the simplest normal case, we assume, as in Example 4.7.1, that the $X_{i}$ are independent normal with mean $\theta_{i}$ and variance $\sigma^{2}$ , and that the $\theta_{i}$ 's are also normal, say with mean $\xi$ and variance A (previously denoted by $\tau^{2}$ ), that is, $\mathbf{X} \sim N_{r}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \sigma^{2}I)$ and $\boldsymbol{\theta} \sim N_{r}(\boldsymbol{\xi}, AI)$ . This model has some similarity with the Model II version of the one-way layout considered in Section 3.5. There, however, interest centered on the variances $\sigma^{2}$ and A, while we now wish to estimate the $\theta_{i}$ 's. 

To simplify the problem, we shall begin by assuming that $\sigma$ and $\xi$ are known, say $\sigma = 1$ and $\xi = 0$ , so that only A and $\theta$ are unknown. The empirical Bayes arguments of Example 4.7.1 led to the estimator 

$$
\delta_ {i} ^ {\hat {\pi}} = (1 - \hat {B}) x _ {i},\tag{5.1}
$$

where $\hat{B}=(r-2)/\Sigma x_{i}^{2}$ , that is, the James-Stein estimator (4.21) with $\mu=0$ . We now prove that, as previously claimed, the risk function of (5.1) is given by (4.25). However, we shall do so for the more general estimator (5.1) with $\hat{B}=c(r-2)/\Sigma x_{i}^{2}$ where c is a positive constant. (The value c=1 minimizes both the Bayes risk (Problem 4.7.5) and the frequentist risk among estimators of this form.) 

Theorem 5.1 Let $X_{i}, i = 1, \ldots, r (r > 2)$ , be independent, with distributions $N(\theta_{i}, 1)$ and let the estimator $\delta_{c}$ of $\theta$ be given by 

$$
\delta_ {c} (\mathbf {x}) = \left(1 - c \frac {r - 2}{| \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}}\right) \mathbf {x}, \quad | \mathbf {x} | ^ {2} = \Sigma x _ {j} ^ {2}.\tag{5.2}
$$

Then, the risk function of $\delta_c$ , with loss function (5.17), is 

$$
R (\pmb {\theta}, \delta_ {c}) = 1 - \frac {(r - 2) ^ {2}}{r} E _ {\theta} \left[ \frac {c (2 - c)}{| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2}} \right].\tag{5.3}
$$

Proof. From Theorem 4.7.2, using the loss function (4.17), the risk of $\delta_c$ is 

$$
R (\pmb {\theta}, \delta_ {c}) = 1 + \frac {1}{r} E _ {\theta} | g (\mathbf {X}) | ^ {2} - \frac {2}{r} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} E _ {\theta} \frac {\partial}{\partial X _ {i}} g _ {i} (\mathbf {X})\tag{5.4}
$$

where $g_{i}(\mathbf{x}) = c(r - 2)x_{i} / |\mathbf{x}|^{2}$ and $|g(\mathbf{x})|^{2} = c^{2}(r - 2)^{2} / |\mathbf{x}|^{2}$ . Differentiation shows 

$$
\frac {\partial}{\partial x _ {i}} g _ {i} (\mathbf {x}) = \frac {c (r - 2)}{| \mathbf {x} | ^ {4}} [ | \mathbf {x} | ^ {2} - 2 x _ {i} ^ {2} ]\tag{5.5}
$$

and hence 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} \frac {\partial}{\partial x _ {i}} g _ {i} (\mathbf {x}) = \frac {c (r - 2)}{| \mathbf {x} | ^ {4}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} [ | \mathbf {x} | ^ {2} - 2 x _ {i} ^ {2} ] \\ = \frac {c (r - 2)}{| \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}} (r - 2), \end{array}
$$

and substitution into (5.4) gives 

$$
\begin{array}{c} R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta_ {c}) = 1 + \frac {1}{r} E _ {\theta} \left[ \frac {c ^ {2} (r - 2) ^ {2}}{| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2}} \right] - \frac {2}{r} E _ {\theta} \left[ \frac {c (r - 2) ^ {2}}{| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2}} \right] \\ = 1 - \frac {(r - 2) ^ {2}}{r} E _ {\theta} \left[ \frac {c (2 - c)}{| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2}} \right]. \end{array}
$$

Note that 

$$
E _ {\theta} \left[ \frac {1}{| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2}} \right] \leq E _ {0} \left[ \frac {1}{| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2}} \right],\tag{5.6}
$$

so $R(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \delta_c) < \infty$ only if the latter expectation is finite, which occurs when $r \geq 3$ (see Problem 5.2).

where $(\cdot)^{+}$ indicates that the quantity in parentheses is replaced by 0 whenever it is negative. We shall call

the positive part of $(\cdot)$ . The risk functions of the ordinary and positive-part Stein estimators are shown in Figure 5.1.

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/70dfd373-7d91-42c2-813a-29f39673925b/dd46cce95e0c76c44f441c07760d7448b45c666df9575e1881d7f5eeee8189d3.jpg)


Unfortunately, it can be shown that even $\delta^{+}$ is inadmissible because it is not smooth enough to be either Bayes or limiting Bayes, as we will see in Section 5.7. However, as suggested by Efron and Morris (1973a, Section 5), the positive-part estimator $\delta^{+}$ is difficult to dominate, and it took another twenty years until a dominating estimator was found by Shao and Strawderman (1994). There exist, in fact, many admissible minimax estimators, but they are of a more general form than (5.1) or (5.9). To obtain such an estimator, we state the following generalization of Corollary 5.2, due to Baranchik (1970) (see also Strawderman 1971, and Efron and Morris 1976a). The proof is left to Problem 5.4. 

Theorem 5.5 For $\mathbf{X} \sim N_r(\boldsymbol{\theta}, I)$ , $r \geq 3$ , and loss $L(\boldsymbol{\theta}, d) = \frac{1}{r} \Sigma(d_i - \theta_i)^2$ , an estimator of the form 

$$
\delta_ {i} = \left[ 1 - c (| \mathbf {x} |) \frac {r - 2}{| \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}} \right] x _ {i}\tag{5.10}
$$

is minimax provided 

(i) $0 \leq c(\cdot) \leq 2$ and 

(ii) the function $c$ is nondecreasing. 

It is interesting to note how very different the situation for $r \geq 3$ is from the one-dimensional problem discussed in Sections 5.2 and 5.3. There, minimax estimators were unique (although recall Example 2.9); here, they constitute a rich collection. It follows from Theorem 5.4 that the estimators (5.10) are inadmissible whenever $c(|\mathbf{x}|)/|\mathbf{x}|^{2} > 1/(r-2)$ with positive probability. On the other hand, the family (5.10) does contain some admissible members, as is shown by the following example, due to Strawderman (1971). 

Example 5.6 Proper Bayes minimax. Let $X_{i}$ be independent normal with mean $\theta_{i}$ and unit variance, and suppose that the $\theta_{i}$ 's are themselves random variables with the following two-stage prior distribution. For a fixed value of $\lambda$ , let the $\theta_{i}$ be iid according to $N[0, \lambda^{-1}(1 - \lambda)]$ . In addition, suppose that $\lambda$ itself is a random variable, $\Lambda$ , with distribution $\Lambda \sim (1 - a)\lambda^{-a}$ , $0 \leq a < 1$ . We therefore have the hierarchical model 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbf {X} \sim N _ {r} (\boldsymbol {\theta}, I), \\ \boldsymbol {\theta} \sim N _ {r} (0, \lambda^ {- 1} (1 - \lambda) I), \\ \Lambda \sim (1 - a) \lambda^ {- a}, \quad 0 <   \lambda <   1, \quad 0 <   a <   1. \end{array}\tag{5.11}
$$

Here, for illustration, we take a = 0 so that $\Lambda$ has the uniform distribution $U(0, 1)$ . A straightforward calculation (Problem 5.5) shows that the Bayes estimator $\delta$ , under squared error loss (4.17), is given by (5.10) with 

$$
c (| \mathbf {x} |) = \frac {1}{r - 2} \left[ r + 2 - \frac {2 \exp \left(- \frac {1}{2} | \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}\right)}{\int_ {0} ^ {1} \lambda^ {r / 2} \exp \left(- \lambda | \mathbf {x} | ^ {2} / 2\right) d \lambda} \right].\tag{5.12}
$$

It follows from Problem 5.4 that $E(\Lambda |\mathbf{x}) = (r - 2)c(|\mathbf{x}|) / |\mathbf{x}|^2$ and hence that $c(|\mathbf{x}|) \geq 0$ since $\lambda < 1$ . On the other hand, $c(|\mathbf{x}|) \leq (r + 2) / (r - 2)$ and hence $c(|\mathbf{x}|) \leq 2$ provided $r \geq 6$ . It remains to show that $c(|\mathbf{x}|)$ is nondecreasing or, equivalently, that 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {1} \lambda^ {r / 2} \exp \left[ \frac {1}{2} | \mathbf {x} | ^ {2} (1 - \lambda) \right] d \lambda
$$

is nondecreasing in $|\mathbf{x}|$ . This is obvious since $0 < \lambda < 1$ . 

Thus, the estimator (5.10) with $c(|\mathbf{x}|)$ given by (5.12) is a proper Bayes (and admissible) minimax estimator for $r \geq 6$ . 

Although neither the James-Stein estimator nor its positive-part version of $(5.9)$ are admissible, it appears that no substantial improvements over the latter are possible (see Example 7.3). We shall now turn to some generalizations of these estimators, where we no longer require equal variances or equal weights in the loss function. 

We first look at the case where the covariance matrix is no longer $\sigma^{2}I$ , but may be any positive definite matrix $\Sigma$ . Conditions for minimaxity of the estimator 

$$
\delta (\mathbf {x}) = \left(1 - \frac {c (| \mathbf {x} | ^ {2})}{| \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}}\right) \mathbf {x}\tag{5.13}
$$

will now involve this covariance matrix. 

Theorem 5.7 For $\mathbf{X} \sim N_r(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \Sigma)$ with $\Sigma$ known, an estimator of the form (5.13) is minimax against the loss $L(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \delta) = |\boldsymbol{\theta} - \delta|^2$ , provided 

$$
(i) 0 \leq c (| \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}) \leq 2 [ \mathrm{tr} (\Sigma) / \lambda_ {\max} (\Sigma) ] - 4,
$$

(ii) the function $c(\cdot)$ is nondecreasing, 

where $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)$ denotes the trace of the matrix $\Sigma$ and $\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)$ denotes its largest eigenvalue. 

Note that the covariance matrix must satisfy $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)/\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma) > 2$ for $\delta$ to be different from X. If $\Sigma = I$ , $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)/\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma) = r$ , so this is the dimensionality restriction in another guise. Bock (1975) (see also Brown 1975) shows that X is unique minimax among spherically symmetric estimators if $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)/\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma) < 2$ . (An estimator is said to be spherically symmetric if it is equivariant under orthogonal transformations. Such estimators were characterized by (4.11), to which (5.13) is equivalent.) 

When the bound on $c(\cdot)$ is displayed in terms of the covariance matrix, we get some idea of the types of problems in which we can expect improvement from shrinkage estimators. The condition $\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma) > 2\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)$ will be satisfied when the eigenvalues of $\Sigma$ are not too different (see Problem 5.10). If this condition is not satisfied, then estimators which allow different coordinatewise shrinkage are needed to obtain minimaxity (see Notes 9.6). 

Proof of Theorem 5.7. The risk of $\delta (\mathbf{x})$ is 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & R (\pmb {\theta}, \delta) = E _ {\theta} \left[ (\pmb {\theta} - \delta (\mathbf {X})) ^ {\prime} (\pmb {\theta} - \delta (\mathbf {X})) \right] \\ & \quad = E _ {\theta} \left[ (\pmb {\theta} - \mathbf {X}) ^ {\prime} (\pmb {\theta} - \mathbf {X}) \right] \\ & \qquad - 2 E _ {\theta} \left[ \frac {c (| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2})}{| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2}} \mathbf {X} ^ {\prime} (\pmb {\theta} - \mathbf {X}) \right] + E _ {\theta} \left[ \frac {c ^ {2} (| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2})}{| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2}} \right] \end{array}\tag{5.14}
$$

where $E_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\mathbf{X})'(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\mathbf{X})=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)$ , the trace of the matrix $\Sigma$ , is the minimax risk (Problem 5.8). We can now apply integration by parts (see Problem 5.9) to write 

$$
\begin{array}{c} R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) = \operatorname{tr} (\Sigma) + E _ {\theta} \left\{\frac {c (| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2})}{| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2}} \left[ (c (| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2}) + 4) \frac {\mathbf {X} ^ {\prime} \Sigma \mathbf {X}}{| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2}} - 2 \operatorname{tr} \Sigma \right] \right\} \\ - 4 E _ {\theta} \frac {c ^ {\prime} (| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2})}{| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2}} \mathbf {X} ^ {\prime} \Sigma \mathbf {X}. \end{array}\tag{5.15}
$$

Since $c'(\cdot) \geq 0$ , an upper bound on $R(\theta, \delta)$ results by dropping the last term. We 

[5.5 

then note [see Equation (2.6.5)] 

$$
\frac {\mathbf {x} ^ {\prime} \boldsymbol {\Sigma} \mathbf {x}}{| \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}} = \frac {\mathbf {x} ^ {\prime} \boldsymbol {\Sigma} \mathbf {x}}{\mathbf {x} ^ {\prime} \mathbf {x}} \leq \lambda_ {\max} (\boldsymbol {\Sigma})\tag{5.16}
$$

and the result follows. 

Theorem 5.5 can also be extended by considering more general loss functions in which the coordinates may have different weights. 

Example 5.8 Loss functions in the one-way layout. In the one-way layout we observe 

$$
X _ {i j} \sim N (\xi_ {i}, \sigma_ {i} ^ {2}), j = 1, \ldots , n _ {i}, i = 1, \ldots , r,\tag{5.17}
$$

where the usual estimator of $\xi_{i}$ is $\bar{X}_{i} = \sum_{j} X_{ij} / n_{i}$ . If the assumptions of Theorem 5.7 are satisfied, then the estimator $\bar{\mathbf{X}} = (\bar{X}_{1}, \ldots, \bar{X}_{r})$ can be improved. If the $\xi_{i}$ 's represent mean responses for different treatments, for example, crop yields from different fertilization treatments or mean responses from different drug therapies, it may be unrealistic to penalize the estimation of each coordinate by the same amount. In particular, if one drug is uncommonly expensive or if a fertilization treatment is quite difficult to apply, this could be reflected in the loss function. 

The situation described in Example 5.8 can be generalized to 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathbf {X} \sim N (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \Sigma), \\ L (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) = (\boldsymbol {\theta} - \delta) ^ {\prime} Q (\boldsymbol {\theta} - \delta), \end{array}\tag{5.18}
$$

where both $\Sigma$ and $Q$ are positive definite matrices. We again ask under what conditions the estimator (5.13) is a minimax estimator of $\theta$ . 

Before answering this question, we first note that, without loss of generality, we can consider one of $\Sigma$ or Q to be the identity (see Problem 5.11). Hence, we take $\Sigma = I$ in the following theorem, whose proof is left to Problem 5.12; see also Problem 5.13 for a more general result. 

Theorem 5.9 Let $\mathbf{X} \sim N(\boldsymbol{\theta}, I)$ . An estimator of the form (5.13) is minimax against the loss $L(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \delta) = (\boldsymbol{\theta} - \delta)'Q(\boldsymbol{\theta} - \delta)$ , provided 

$$
(i) 0 \leq c (| \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}) \leq 2 [ \operatorname{tr} (Q) / \lambda_ {\max} (Q) ] - 4,
$$

(ii) the function $c(\cdot)$ is nondecreasing. 

Theorem 5.9 can also be viewed as a robustness result, since we have shown $\delta$ to be minimax against any $Q$ , which provides an upper bound for $c(|\mathbf{x}|^2)$ in (i). This is in the same spirit as the results of Brown (1975), mentioned in Section 5.5. (See Problem 5.14.) 

Thus far, we have been mainly concerned with one form of shrinkage estimator, the estimator (5.13). We shall now obtain a more general class of minimax estimators by writing $\delta$ as $\delta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x} - g(\mathbf{x})$ and utilizing the resulting expression (5.4) for the risk of $\delta$ . As first noted by Stein, (5.4) can be combined with the identities derived in Section 4.3 (for the Bayes estimator in an exponential family) to obtain a set of sufficient conditions for minimaxity in terms of the condition of superharmonicity of the marginal distribution (see Section 1.7). 

In particular, for the case of $\mathbf{X} \sim N(\boldsymbol{\theta}, I)$ , we can, by Corollary 3.3, write a Bayes estimator of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ as 

$$
E (\theta_ {i} | \mathbf {x}) = \frac {\partial}{\partial x _ {i}} \log m (\mathbf {x}) - \frac {\partial}{\partial x _ {i}} \log h (\mathbf {x})\tag{5.19}
$$

with $-\partial \log h(\mathbf{x}) / \partial x_{i} = x_{i}$ (Problem 5.17) so that the Bayes estimators are of the form 

$$
\delta (\mathbf {x}) = \mathbf {x} + \nabla \log m (\mathbf {x}).\tag{5.20}
$$

Theorem 5.10 If $\mathbf{X} \sim N_r(\theta, I)$ , the risk, under squared error loss, of the estimator (5.20) is given by 

$$
\begin{array}{c} R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) = 1 + \frac {4}{r} E _ {\theta} \left\{\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} \frac {\frac {\partial^ {2}}{\partial x _ {i} ^ {2}} \sqrt {m (\mathbf {X})}}{\sqrt {m (\mathbf {X})}} \right\} \\ = 1 + \frac {4}{r} E _ {\theta} \frac {\nabla^ {2} \sqrt {m (\mathbf {X})}}{\sqrt {m (\mathbf {X})}} \end{array}\tag{5.21}
$$

where $\nabla^2 f = \sum \{(\partial^2 /\partial x_i^2)f\}$ is the Laplacian of $f$ 

Proof. The $i$ th component of the estimator (5.20) is 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \delta_ {i} (\mathbf {x}) & = x _ {i} + (\nabla \log m (\mathbf {x})) _ {i} \\ & = x _ {i} + \frac {\partial}{\partial x _ {i}} \log m (\mathbf {x}) = x _ {i} + \frac {m _ {i} ^ {\prime} (\mathbf {x})}{m (\mathbf {x})} \end{array}
$$

where, for simplicity of notation, we write $m_i'(\mathbf{x}) = (\partial/\partial x_i)m(\mathbf{x})$ . In the risk identity (5.4), set $g_i(\mathbf{x}) = -m_i'(\mathbf{x})/m(\mathbf{x})$ to obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) = 1 + \frac {1}{r} E _ {\theta} \left\{\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} \left[ \frac {m _ {i} ^ {\prime} (\mathbf {X})}{m (\mathbf {X})} \right] ^ {2} \right\} + \frac {2}{r} E _ {\theta} \left\{\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} \left[ \frac {\partial}{\partial x _ {i}} \frac {m _ {i} ^ {\prime} (\mathbf {X})}{m (\mathbf {X})} \right] \right\} \\ = 1 + \frac {1}{r} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} E _ {\theta} \left\{2 \frac {m _ {i} ^ {\prime \prime} (\mathbf {X})}{m (\mathbf {X})} - \left[ \frac {m _ {i} ^ {\prime} (\mathbf {X})}{m (\mathbf {X})} \right] ^ {2} \right\} \end{array}\tag{5.22}
$$

where $m_{i}^{\prime\prime}(\mathbf{x}) = (\partial^{2}/\partial x_{i}^{2})m(\mathbf{x})$ , and the second expression follows from straightforward differentiation and gathering of terms. Finally, notice the differentiation identity 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {2}}{\partial x _ {i} ^ {2}} [ g (\mathbf {x}) ] ^ {1 / 2} = \frac {g _ {i} ^ {\prime \prime} (\mathbf {x})}{2 [ g (\mathbf {x}) ] ^ {1 / 2}} - \frac {[ g _ {i} ^ {\prime} (\mathbf {x}) ] ^ {2}}{4 [ g (\mathbf {x}) ] ^ {3 / 2}}.\tag{5.23}
$$

Using (5.23), we can rewrite the risk (5.22) in the form (5.21). 

The form of the risk function (5.21) shows that the estimator (5.20) is minimax (provided all expectations are finite) if $\sum(\partial^{2}/\partial x_{i}^{2})[m(\mathbf{x})]^{1/2} < 0$ , and hence by Theorem 1.7.24 if $[m(\mathbf{x})]^{1/2}$ is superharmonic. We, therefore, have established the following class of minimax estimators. 

Corollary 5.11 Under the conditions of Theorem 5.10, if $E_{\theta}\{\nabla^2\sqrt{m(\mathbf{X})} / \sqrt{m(\mathbf{X})}\} < \infty$ and $[m(\mathbf{x})]^{1/2}$ is a superharmonic function, then $\delta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x} + \log \nabla m(\mathbf{x})$ is minimax. 

A useful consequence of Corollary 5.11 follows from the fact that superharmonicity of $m(\mathbf{x})$ implies that of $[m(\mathbf{x})]^{1/2}$ (Problem 1.7.16) and is often easier to verify. 

Corollary 5.12 Under the conditions of Theorem 5.10, if $E_{\theta}|\nabla m(\mathbf{X}) / m(\mathbf{X})|^2 < \infty$ , $E_{\theta}|\nabla^2 m(\mathbf{X}) / m(\mathbf{X})| < \infty$ , and $m(\mathbf{x})$ is a superharmonic function, then $\delta (\mathbf{x}) = x + \log \nabla m(\mathbf{x})$ is minimax. 

Proof. From the second expression in (5.22), we see that 

$$
R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) \leq 1 + \frac {2}{r} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} E _ {\theta} \frac {m _ {i} ^ {\prime \prime} (\mathbf {X})}{m (\mathbf {X})},\tag{5.24}
$$

which is $\leq 1$ if $m(\mathbf{x})$ is superharmonic. 

Example 5.13 Superharmonicity of the marginal. For the model in (5.11) of Example 5.6, we have 

$$
m (\mathbf {x}) \propto \int_ {0} ^ {1} \lambda^ {(r / 2) - a} e ^ {\frac {- \lambda}{2} | \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}} d \lambda
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} \frac {\partial^ {2}}{\partial x _ {i} ^ {2}} m (\mathbf {x}) \propto \int_ {0} ^ {1} \lambda^ {(r / 2) - a + 1} [ \lambda | \mathbf {x} | ^ {2} - r ] e ^ {\frac {- \lambda}{2} | \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}} d \lambda \\ \qquad = \frac {1}{(| \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}) ^ {(r / 2) - a + 2}} \int_ {0} ^ {| \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}} t ^ {(r / 2) - a + 1} [ t - r ] e ^ {- t / 2} d t. \end{array}\tag{5.25}
$$

Thus, a sufficient condition for $m(\mathbf{x})$ to be superharmonic is 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {| \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}} t ^ {(r / 2) - a + 1} [ t - r ] e ^ {- t / 2} d t \leq 0.\tag{5.26}
$$

From Problem 5.18, we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {0} ^ {| \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}} t ^ {(r / 2) - a + 1} [ t - r ] e ^ {- t / 2} d t \leq \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} t ^ {(r / 2) - a + 1} [ t - r ] e ^ {- t / 2} d t \\ = \Gamma \left(\frac {r}{2} - a + 2\right) 2 ^ {(r / 2) - a + 2} [ - 2 a + 4 ], \end{array}\tag{5.27}
$$

so $m(\mathbf{x})$ is superharmonic if $-2a + 4 \leq 0$ or $a \geq 2$ . For the choice $a = 2$ , the Strawderman estimator is (Problem 5.5) 

$$
\delta (\mathbf {x}) = \left(1 - \frac {r - 2}{| \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}} \left[ \frac {P \left(\chi_ {r} ^ {2} \leq | \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}\right)}{P \left(\chi_ {r - 2} ^ {2} \leq | \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}\right)} \right]\right) \mathbf {x},
$$

which resembles the positive-part Stein estimator. Note that this estimator is not a proper Bayes estimator, as the prior distribution is improper. 

There are many other characterizations of superharmonic functions that lead to different versions of minimax theorems. A most useful one, noticed by Stein (1981), is the following. 

Corollary 5.14 Under the conditions of Theorem 5.10 and Corollary 5.11, if the prior $\pi(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ is superharmonic, then $\delta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x} + \nabla \log m(\mathbf{x})$ is minimax. 

Proof. The marginal density can be written as 

$$
m (\mathbf {x}) = \int \phi_ {r} (\mathbf {x} - \pmb {\theta}) \pi (\pmb {\theta}) d \pmb {\theta},\tag{5.28}
$$

where $\phi_r(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\theta})$ is the $r$ -variate normal density. From Problem 1.7.16, the superharmonicity of $m(\mathbf{x})$ follows. 

Example 5.15 Superharmonic prior. The hierarchical Bayes estimators of Faith (1978) (Problem 5.7) are based on the multivariate t prior 

$$
\pi (\boldsymbol {\theta}) \propto \left(\frac {2}{b} + | \boldsymbol {\theta} | ^ {2}\right) ^ {- (a + r / 2)}.\tag{5.29}
$$

It is straightforward to verify that this prior is superharmonic if $a \leq -1$ , allowing a simple verification of minimaxity of an estimator that can only be expressed as an integral. 

The superharmonic condition, although sometimes difficult to verify, has often proved helpful in not only establishing minimaxity but also in understanding what types of prior distributions may lead to minimax Bayes estimators. See Note 9.7 for further discussion. 

We close this section with an examination of componentwise risk. For $X_{i} \sim N(\theta_{i}, 1)$ , independent, and risk function 

$$
\bar {R} (\pmb {\theta}, \delta) = \frac {1}{r} \Sigma R (\theta_ {i}, \delta_ {i})\tag{5.30}
$$

with $R(\theta_i, \delta_i) = E(\delta_i - \theta_i)^2$ , it was seen in Section 5.3 that it is not possible to find a $\delta_i$ for which $R(\theta_i, \delta_i)$ is uniformly better than $R(\theta_i, X_i) = 1$ . 

Thus, the improvement in the average risk can be achieved only though increasing some of the component risks, and it becomes of interest to consider the maximum possible component risk 

$$
\max _ {i} \sup _ {\theta_ {i}} R (\theta_ {i}, \delta_ {i}).\tag{5.31}
$$

For given $\lambda = \Sigma\theta_{j}^{2}$ , it can be shown (Baranchik 1964) that (5.31) attains its maximum when all but one of the $\theta_{i}$ 's are zero, say $\theta_{2} = \cdots = \theta_{r} = 0$ , $\theta_{1} = \sqrt{\lambda}$ , and that this maximum risk $\rho_{r}(\lambda)$ as a function of $\lambda$ increases from a minimum of 2/r at $\lambda = 0$ to a maximum and then decreases and tends to 1 as $\lambda \to \infty$ ; see Figure 6.2. 

The values of $\max_{\lambda}\rho_{r}(\lambda)$ and the value $\lambda_{r}$ at which the maximum is attained, shown in Table 5.1, are given by Efron and Morris (1972a). The table suggests that shrinkage estimators will typically not be appropriate when the component problems concern different clients. No one wants his or her blood test subjected to the possibility of large errors in order to improve a laboratory's average performance. 

To get a feeling for the behavior of the James-Stein estimator (4.21) with $\mu = 0$ , in a situation in which most of the $\theta_{i}$ 's are at or near zero (representing the standard or normal situation of no effect) but a few relatively large $\theta_{i}$ 's are present, consider the 20-component model

$$

where $\lambda = |\theta|^{2}$ (see Problem 5.23). Its values are given in Table 5.2.

To see the effect of the shrinkage explicitly, suppose, for example, that the observation $X_{20}$ corresponding to $\theta_{20}=2$ turned out to be 2.71. The modified estimate ranges from $2.71\times.17=.46$ (when $\theta_{1}=\cdots=\theta_{19}=0$ ) to $2.71\times.66=1.79$ (when $\theta_{1}=\cdots=\theta_{17}=0$ , $\theta_{18}=\theta_{19}=4$ ). 

What is seen here can be summarized roughly as follows: 

(i) If all the $\theta_{i}$ 's are at or fairly close to zero, then the James-Stein estimator will reduce the $\mathbf{X}$ 's very substantially in absolute value and thereby typically will greatly improve the accuracy of the estimated values. 

(ii) If there are some very large $\theta_{i}$ 's or a substantial number of moderate ones, the factor by which the $\mathbf{X}$ 's are multiplied will not be very far from 1, and the modification will not have a great effect. 

Neither of these situations causes much of a problem: In (ii), the modification presents an unnecessary but not particularly harmful complication; in (i), it is clearly very beneficial. The danger arises in the following intermediate situation. 

(iii) Most of the $\theta_{i}$ 's are close to zero, but there are a few moderately large $\theta_{i}$ 's (of the order of two to four standard deviations, say). These represent the cases in which something is going on, about which we will usually want to know. However, in these cases, the estimated values are heavily shrunk toward the norm, with the resulting risk of their being found “innocent by association.” 

If one is interested in minimizing the average risk (5.30) but is concerned about the possibility of large component risks, a compromise is possible along the lines of restricted Bayes estimation mentioned in Section 5.2. One can impose an upper bound on the maximum component risk, say 10% or 25% above the minimax risk of 1 (when $\sigma = 1$ ). Subject to this restriction, one can then try to minimize the average risk, for example, in the sense of obtaining a Bayes or empirical Bayes solution. An approximation to such an approach has been developed by Efron and Morris (1971, 1972a), Berger (1982a, 1988b), Bickel (1983, 1984), and Kempthorne (1988a, 1988b). See Example 6.7 for an illustration. 

The results discussed in this and the preceding section for the simultaneous estimation of normal means have been extended, particularly to various members of the exponential family and to general location parameter families, with and without nuisance parameters. The next section contains a number of illustrations. 

## 6 Extensions

The estimators of the previous section have all been constructed for the case of the estimation of $\theta$ based on observing $\mathbf{X} \sim N_{r}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, I)$ . The applicability of shrinkage estimation, now often referred to as Stein estimation, goes far beyond this case. In this section, through examples, we will try to illustrate some of the wide ranging applicability of the “Stein effect,” that is, the ability to improve individual estimates by using ensemble information. 

Also, the shrinkage estimators previously considered were designed to obtain the greatest risk improvement in a specified region of the parameter space. For example, the maximum risk improvement of $(5.10)$ occurs at $\theta_{1} = \theta_{2} = \cdots = \theta_{r} = 0$ , while that of $(4.21)$ occurs at $\theta_{1} = \mu_{1}, \theta_{2} = \mu_{2}, \ldots, \theta_{r} = \mu_{r}$ . In the next three examples, we look at modifications of Stein estimators that shrink toward adaptively chosen targets, that is, targets selected by the data. By doing so, it is hoped that a maximal risk improvement will be realized. 

Although we only touch upon the topic of selecting a shrinkage target, the literature is vast. See Note 9.7 for some references. 

The first two examples examine estimators that we have seen before, in the context of empirical Bayes analysis of variance and regression (Examples 4.7.7 and 4.7.8). These estimators shrink toward subspaces of the parameter space rather than specified points. Moreover, we can allow the data to help choose the specific shrinkage target. We now establish minimaxity of such estimators. 

Example 6.1 Shrinking toward a common mean. In problems where it is thought there is some similarity between components, a reasonable choice of shrinkage target may be the linear subspace where all the components are equal. This was illustrated in Example 4.7.7, where the estimator (4.7.28) shrunk the coordinates toward an estimated common mean value rather than a specified point. 

For the average squared error loss $L(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \delta) = \frac{1}{r} |\boldsymbol{\theta} - \delta|^2$ , the estimator (4.7.28) with coordinates 

$$
\delta_ {i} ^ {L} (\mathbf {x}) = \bar {x} + \left(1 - \frac {c (r - 3)}{\sum_ {j} (x _ {j} - \bar {x}) ^ {2}}\right) (x _ {i} - \bar {x}),\tag{6.1}
$$

has risk given by 

$$
R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta^ {L}) = 1 + \frac {(r - 3) ^ {2}}{r} E _ {\theta} \left[ \frac {c (c - 2)}{\sum_ {j} (X _ {j} - \bar {X}) ^ {2}} \right].\tag{6.2}
$$

Hence, $\delta^{L}$ is minimax if $r \geq 4$ and $c \leq 2$ . The minimum risk is attained at $\theta$ values that satisfy $\sum(\theta_{i} - \bar{\theta})^{2} = 0$ , that is, where $\theta_{1} = \theta_{2} = \cdots = \theta_{r}$ . Moreover, the best value of c is c = 1, which results in a minimum risk of 3/r. This is greater than the minimum of 2/r (for the case of a known value of $\theta$ ) but is attained on a larger set. See Problems 6.1 and 6.2. 

Example 6.2 Shrinking toward a linear subspace. The estimator $\delta^{L}$ given by (6.1) shrinks toward the subspace of the parameter space defined by 

$$
\mathcal {L} = \left\{\boldsymbol {\theta}: \theta_ {1} = \theta_ {2} = \dots = \theta_ {r} \right\} = \left\{\boldsymbol {\theta}: \frac {1}{r} J \boldsymbol {\theta} = \boldsymbol {\theta} \right\}\tag{6.3}
$$

where J is a matrix of 1's, $J = 11'$ . 

Another useful submodel, which is a generalization of $(6.3)$ , is 

$$
\theta_ {i} = \alpha + \beta t _ {i}\tag{6.4}
$$

where the $t_i$ 's are known but $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are unknown. This corresponds to the (sub)model of a linear trend in the means (see Example 4.7.8). If we define 

$$
T = \binom{1 1 \dots 1}{t _ {1} t _ {2} \dots t _ {r}} ^ {\prime},\tag{6.5}
$$

then the $\theta_{i}$ 's satisfying (6.4) constitute the subspace 

$$
\mathcal {L} = \left\{\boldsymbol {\theta}: T ^ {*} \boldsymbol {\theta} = \boldsymbol {\theta} \right\},\tag{6.6}
$$

where $T^{*} = T(T'T)^{-1}T'$ is the matrix that projects any vector $\theta$ into the subspace. (Such projection matrices are symmetric and idempotent, that is, they satisfy $(T^{*})^{2} = I$ .) 

The models (6.3) and (6.6) suggest what the more general situation would look like when the target is a linear subspace defined by 

$$
\mathcal {L} _ {k} = \{\boldsymbol {\theta}: K \boldsymbol {\theta} = \boldsymbol {\theta}, \quad K \text {   idempotent   of   rank   } s \}.\tag{6.7}
$$

If we shrink toward the MLE of $\theta \in L_{k}$ , which is given by $\hat{\theta}_{k} = Kx$ , the resulting Stein estimator is 

$$
\delta^ {k} (\mathbf {x}) = \hat {\boldsymbol {\theta}} _ {k} + \left(1 - \frac {r - s - 2}{| \mathbf {x} - \hat {\boldsymbol {\theta}} _ {k} | ^ {2}}\right) (\mathbf {x} - \hat {\boldsymbol {\theta}} _ {k})\tag{6.8}
$$

and is minimax provided $r - s > 2$ . (See Problem 6.3.) More general linear restrictions are possible: one can take $\mathcal{L} = \{\pmb{\theta} : H\pmb{\theta} = m\}$ where $H_{s \times r}$ and $m_{s \times 1}$ are specified (see Casella and Hwang, 1987). 

Example 6.3 Combining biased and unbiased estimators. Green and Strawderman (1991) show how the Stein effect can be used to combine biased and unbiased estimators, and they apply their results to a problem in forestry. 

An important attribute of a forest stand (a homogeneous group of trees) is the basal area per acre, B, defined as the sum of the cross-sectional areas 4.5 feet above the ground of all trees. Regression models exist that predict $\log B$ as a function of stand age, number of trees per acre, and the average height of the dominant trees in the stand. The average prediction, Y, from the regression is a biased estimator of B. Green and Strawderman investigated how to combine this estimator with X, the sample mean basal area from a small sample of trees, to obtain an improved estimator of B. They formulated the problem in the following way. 

Suppose $\mathbf{X} \sim N_{r}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \sigma^{2}I)$ and $\mathbf{Y} \sim N_{r}(\boldsymbol{\theta} + \boldsymbol{\xi}, \tau^{2}I)$ , independent, where $\sigma^{2}$ and $\tau^{2}$ are known, and the loss function is $L(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \delta) = |\boldsymbol{\theta} - \delta|^{2}/r\sigma^{2}$ . Thus, $\xi$ is an unknown nuisance parameter. The estimator 

$$
\delta^ {c} (\mathbf {x}, \mathbf {y}) = \mathbf {y} + \left(1 - \frac {c (r - 2) \sigma^ {2}}{| \mathbf {x} - \mathbf {y} | ^ {2}}\right) (\mathbf {x} - \mathbf {y})\tag{6.9}
$$

is a minimax estimator of $\theta$ if $0 \leq c \leq 2$ , which follows from noting that 

$$
R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta^ {c}) = 1 - \sigma^ {2} \frac {(r - 2) ^ {2}}{r} E \frac {c (2 - c)}{| \mathbf {X} - \mathbf {Y} | ^ {2}}\tag{6.10}
$$

and that the minimax risk is 1. If $\pmb{\xi} = 0$ and, hence, $\mathbf{Y}$ is also an unbiased estimator of $\pmb{\theta}$ , then the optimal linear combined estimator 

$$
\delta^ {\mathrm{comb}} (\mathbf {x}, \mathbf {y}) = \frac {\tau^ {2} \mathbf {x} + \sigma^ {2} \mathbf {y}}{\sigma^ {2} + \tau^ {2}}\tag{6.11}
$$

dominates $\delta^1 (\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$ in risk. However, the risk of $\delta^{\mathrm{comb}}$ becomes unbounded as $|\pmb {\xi}|\to \infty$ , whereas that of $\delta^1$ is bounded by 1. (See Problems 6.5 and 6.6.) 

The next example looks at the important case of unknown variance. 

Example 6.4 Unknown variance. The James-Stein estimator (4.21) which shrinks X toward a given point $\mu$ was obtained under the assumption that $\mathbf{X} \sim N(\boldsymbol{\theta}, I)$ . We shall now generalize this estimator to the situations, first, that the common variance of the $X_{i}$ has a known value $\sigma^{2}$ and then that $\sigma^{2}$ is unknown. 

In the first case, the problem can be reduced to that with unit variance by considering the variables $X_{i}/\sigma$ and estimating the means $\theta_{i}/\sigma$ and then multiplying the estimator of $\theta_{i}/\sigma$ by $\sigma$ to obtain an estimator of $\theta_{i}$ . This argument leads to replacing (4.21) by 

$$
\delta_ {i} = \mu_ {i} + \left(1 - \frac {r - 2}{| {\bf x} - {\pmb \mu} | ^ {2} / \sigma^ {2}}\right) (x _ {i} - \mu_ {i}),\tag{6.12}
$$

where $|\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}|^2 = \Sigma (x_i - \mu_i)^2$ , with risk function (see Problem 6.7) 

$$
R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) = \sigma^ {2} \left[ 1 - \frac {r - 2}{r} E _ {\theta} \left(\frac {r - 2}{| \mathbf {X} - \boldsymbol {\mu} | ^ {2} / \sigma^ {2}}\right) \right].\tag{6.13}
$$

Suppose now that $\sigma^2$ is unknown. We shall then suppose that there exists a random variable $S^2$ , independent of $\mathbf{X}$ and such that $S^2 / \sigma^2 \sim \chi_\nu^2$ , and we shall in (6.12) replace $\sigma^2$ by $\hat{\sigma}^2 = kS^2$ , where $k$ is a positive constant. The estimator is 

then modified to 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \delta_ {i} = \mu_ {i} + \left(1 - \frac {r - 2}{| \mathbf {x} - \boldsymbol {\mu} | ^ {2} / \hat {\sigma} ^ {2}}\right) (x _ {i} - \mu_ {i}) \\ = \mu_ {i} + \left(1 - \frac {r - 2}{| \mathbf {x} - \boldsymbol {\mu} | ^ {2} / \sigma^ {2}} \cdot \frac {\hat {\sigma} ^ {2}}{\sigma^ {2}}\right) (x _ {i} - \mu_ {i}). \end{array}\tag{6.14}
$$

The conditional risk of $\delta$ given $\hat{\sigma}$ is given by (5.4) with $|x - \mu|^{2}$ replaced by $|x - \mu|^{2}/\sigma^{2}$ and $c = \hat{\sigma}^{2}/\sigma^{2}$ . Because of the independence of $S^{2}$ and $|x - \mu|^{2}$ , we thus have 

$$
R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) = 1 - \frac {(r - 2) ^ {2}}{r} E _ {\theta} \left[ \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{| \mathbf {X} - \boldsymbol {\mu} | ^ {2}} \right] E \left[ 2 k \frac {S ^ {2}}{\sigma^ {2}} - k ^ {2} \left(\frac {S ^ {2}}{\sigma^ {2}}\right) ^ {2} \right].\tag{6.15}
$$

Now, $E(S^2 / \sigma^2) = \nu$ and $E(S^2 / \sigma^2)^2 = \nu (\nu + 2)$ , so that the second expectation is 

$$
E \left[ 2 k \frac {S ^ {2}}{\sigma^ {2}} - k ^ {2} \left(\frac {S ^ {2}}{\sigma^ {2}}\right) ^ {2} \right] = 2 k \nu - k ^ {2} \nu (\nu + 2).\tag{6.16}
$$

This is positive (making the estimator minimax) if $k \leq 2/(\nu + 2)$ , and (6.16) is maximized at $k = 1/(\nu + 2)$ where its value is $\nu/(\nu + 2)$ . 

The best choice of k in $\hat{\sigma}^{2}$ thus leads to using the estimator 

$$
\hat {\sigma} ^ {2} = S ^ {2} / (\nu + 2)\tag{6.17}
$$

and the risk of the resulting estimator is 

$$
R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) = 1 - \frac {\nu}{\nu + 2} \frac {(r - 2) ^ {2}}{r} E _ {\theta} \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{| \mathbf {X} - \boldsymbol {\mu} | ^ {2}}.\tag{6.18}
$$

The improvement in risk over X is thus reduced from that of (4.25) by a factor of $\nu/(\nu+2)$ . (See Problems 6.7–6.11.) 

For distributions other than the normal, Strawderman (1974) determined minimax Stein estimators for the following situation. 

Example 6.5 Mixture of normals. Suppose that, given $\sigma$ , the vector X is distributed as $N(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \sigma^{2}I)$ , and that $\sigma$ is a random variable with distribution G, so that the density of X is 

$$
f (| \mathbf {x} - \boldsymbol {\theta} |) = \frac {1}{(2 \pi) ^ {r / 2}} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} e ^ {- (1 / 2 \sigma^ {2}) | \mathbf {x} - \boldsymbol {\theta} | ^ {2}} \sigma^ {- r} d G (\sigma),\tag{6.19}
$$

a scale mixture of normals, including, in particular, the multivariate Student's t-distribution. Since $E(|\mathbf{X}-\boldsymbol{\theta}|^{2} \mid \sigma) = r\sigma^{2}$ , it follows that with loss function $L(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \delta) = |\boldsymbol{\theta} - \delta|^{2}/r$ , the risk of the estimator X is $E(\sigma^{2})$ . On the other hand, the risk of the estimator 

$$
\delta (\mathbf {x}) = \left(1 - \frac {c}{| \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}}\right) \mathbf {x}\tag{6.20}
$$

is given by 

$$
E _ {\theta} L [ \pmb {\theta}, \delta (\mathbf {X}) ] = E _ {\sigma} E _ {\theta | \sigma} L [ \pmb {\theta}, \delta (\mathbf {X}) ].\tag{6.21}
$$

Calculations similar to those in the proofs of Theorems 4.7.2 and 5.1 show that 

$$
E _ {\theta | \sigma} L [ \boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta (\mathbf {X}) ] = \sigma^ {2} - \frac {1}{r} \left[ 2 c (r - 2) - \frac {c ^ {2}}{\sigma^ {2}} \right] E _ {\theta | \sigma} \left(\frac {\sigma^ {2}}{| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2}}\right)
$$

and, hence, 

$$
R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) = E _ {\sigma} \sigma^ {2} - \frac {1}{r} E _ {\sigma} \left\{\left[ 2 c (r - 2) - \frac {c ^ {2}}{\sigma^ {2}} \right] \left[ E _ {\theta | \sigma} \left(\frac {\sigma^ {2}}{| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2}}\right) \right] \right\}.\tag{6.22}
$$

An upper bound on the risk can be obtained from the following lemma, whose proof is left to Problem 6.13. 

Lemma 6.6 Let Y be a random variable, and $g(y)$ and $h(y)$ any functions for which $E[g(Y)]$ , $E[(h(Y)], \text{and } E(g(Y)h(Y))]$ exist. Then: 

(a) If one of the functions $g(\cdot)$ and $h(\cdot)$ is nonincreasing and the other is nondecreasing, 

$$
E [ g (Y) h (Y) ] \leq E [ g (Y) ] E [ h (Y) ].
$$

(b) If both functions are either nondecreasing or nonincreasing, 

$$
E [ g (Y) h (Y) ] \geq E [ g (Y) ] E [ h (Y) ].
$$

Returning to the risk function (6.22), we see that $[2c(r-2)-c^{2}/\sigma^{2}]$ is an increasing function of $\sigma^{2}$ , and $E_{\theta|\sigma}(\sigma^{2}/|\mathbf{X}|^{2})$ is also an increasing function of $\sigma^{2}$ . (This latter statement follows from the fact that, given $\sigma^{2}$ , $|X|^{2}/\sigma^{2}$ has a noncentral $\chi^{2}$ -distribution with noncentrality parameter $|\theta|^{2}/\sigma^{2}$ , and that, therefore, as was pointed out following (4.25), the expectation is increasing in $\sigma^{2}$ .) 

Therefore, by Lemma 6.6, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E _ {\sigma} \left\{\left[ 2 c (r - 2) - \frac {c ^ {2}}{\sigma^ {2}} \right] E _ {\theta | \sigma} \left(\frac {\sigma^ {2}}{| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2}}\right) \right\} \\ \geq E _ {\sigma} \left[ 2 c (r - 2) - \frac {c ^ {2}}{\sigma^ {2}} \right] E _ {\sigma} \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2}} \end{array}
$$

Hence, $\delta (\mathbf{x})$ will dominate $\mathbf{x}$ if 

$$
2 c (r - 2) - c ^ {2} E _ {\sigma} \frac {1}{\sigma^ {2}} \geq 0
$$

or 

$$
0 <   c <   2 (r - 2) / E _ {\sigma} \frac {1}{\sigma^ {2}} = 2 / E _ {0} | \mathbf {X} | ^ {- 2},
$$

where $E_0|\mathbf{X}|^{-2}$ is the expectation when $\theta = 0$ (see Problem 6.12). 

If $f(|\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\theta}|)$ is the normal density $N(\boldsymbol{\theta}, I)$ , then $E_0|\mathbf{X}|^{-2} = (r - 2)^{-1}$ , and we are back to a familiar condition. The interesting fact is that, for a wide class of scale mixtures of normals, $E_0|\mathbf{X}|^{-2} > (r - 2)^{-1}$ . This holds, for example, if $1 / \sigma^2 \sim \chi_\nu^2 / \nu$ so $f(|\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\theta}|)$ is multivariate Student's $t$ . This implies a type of robustness of the estimator (6.20); that is, for $0 \leq c \leq 2(r - 2)$ , $\delta(\mathbf{X})$ dominates 

X under a multivariate t-distribution and hence retains its minimax property (see Problem 6.12). 

Bayes estimators minimize the average risk under the prior, but the maximum of their risk functions can be large and even infinite. On the other hand, minimax estimators often have relatively large Bayes risk under many priors. The following example, due to Berger (1982a), shows how it is sometimes possible to construct estimators having good Bayes risk properties (with respect to a given prior), while at the same time being minimax. The resulting estimator is a compromise between a Bayes estimator and a Stein estimator. 

Example 6.7 Bayesian robustness. For $\mathbf{X} \sim N_r(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \sigma^2 I)$ and $\boldsymbol{\theta} \sim \pi = N_r(0, \tau^2 I)$ , the Bayes estimator against squared error loss is 

$$
\delta^ {\pi} (\mathbf {x}) = \frac {\tau^ {2}}{\sigma^ {2} + \tau^ {2}} \mathbf {x}\tag{6.23}
$$

with Bayes risk $r(\pi, \delta^{\pi}) = r\sigma^{2}\tau^{2} / (\sigma^{2} + \tau^{2})$ . However, $\delta^{\pi}$ is not minimax and, in fact, has unbounded risk (Problem 4.3.12). The Stein estimator 

$$
\delta^ {c} (\mathbf {x}) = \left(1 - c \frac {(r - 2) \sigma^ {2}}{| \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}}\right) \mathbf {x}\tag{6.24}
$$

is minimax if $0 \leq c \leq 2$ , but its Bayes risk 

$$
r (\pi , \delta^ {c}) = r (\pi , \delta^ {\pi}) + \frac {\sigma^ {4}}{\sigma^ {2} + \tau^ {2}} [ r + c (c - 2) (r - 2) ],
$$

at the best value $c = 1$ , is $r(\pi, \delta') = r(\pi, \delta^{\pi}) + 2\sigma^{4} / (\sigma^{2} + \tau^{2})$ . 

To construct a minimax estimator with small Bayes risk, consider the compromise estimator 

$$
\delta^ {R} (\mathbf {x}) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \delta^ {\pi} (\mathbf {x}) & \text { if } | \mathbf {x} | ^ {2} <   c (r - 2) (\sigma^ {2} + \tau^ {2}) \\ \delta^ {c} (\mathbf {x}) & \text { if } | \mathbf {x} | ^ {2} \geq c (r - 2) (\sigma^ {2} + \tau^ {2}). \end{array} \right.\tag{6.25}
$$

This estimator is minimax if $0 \leq c \leq 2$ (Problem 6.14). If $|\mathbf{x}|^{2} > c(r-2)(\sigma^{2} + \tau^{2})$ , the data do not support the prior specification and we, therefore, put $\delta^{R} = \delta^{c}$ ; if $|\mathbf{x}|^{2} < c(r-2)(\sigma^{2} + \tau^{2})$ , we tend to believe that the data support the prior specification since $\frac{|\mathbf{x}|^{2}}{\sigma^{2} + \tau^{2}} \sim \chi_{r}^{2}$ , and we are, therefore, willing to gamble on $\pi$ and put $\delta^{R} = \delta^{\pi}$ . 

The Bayes risk of $\delta^R$ is 

$$
\begin{array}{c} r (\pi , \delta^ {R}) = E | \boldsymbol {\theta} - \delta^ {\pi} (\mathbf {X}) | ^ {2} I \left(| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2} <   c (r - 2) (\sigma^ {2} + \tau^ {2})\right) \\ + E | \boldsymbol {\theta} - \delta^ {c} (\mathbf {X}) | ^ {2} I \left(| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2} \geq c (r - 2) (\sigma^ {2} + \tau^ {2})\right), \end{array}\tag{6.26}
$$

where the expectation is over the joint distribution of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\pmb{\theta}$ . Adding $\pm \delta^{\pi}$ to the second term in (6.26) yields 

$$
\begin{array}{l} r (\pi , \delta^ {R}) = E | \boldsymbol {\theta} - \delta^ {\pi} (\mathbf {X}) | ^ {2} \\ + E | \delta^ {\pi} (\mathbf {X}) - \delta^ {c} (\mathbf {X}) | ^ {2} I \left(| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2} \geq c (r - 2) (\sigma^ {2} + \tau^ {2})\right) \\ = r (\pi , \delta^ {\pi}) + E | \delta^ {\pi} (\mathbf {X}) - \delta^ {c} (\mathbf {X}) | ^ {2} I \left(| \mathbf {X} | ^ {2} \geq c (r - 2) (\sigma^ {2} + \tau^ {2})\right). \end{array}\tag{6.27}
$$

Here, we have used the fact that, marginally, $|\mathbf{X}|^{2}/(\sigma^{2}+\tau^{2})\sim\chi_{r}^{2}$ . We can write (6.27) as (see Problem 6.14) 

$$
\begin{array}{l} r (\pi , \delta^ {R}) = r (\pi , \delta^ {\pi}) \\ \qquad + \frac {1}{r - 2} \frac {\sigma^ {4}}{\sigma^ {2} + \tau^ {2}} E [ Y - c (r - 2) ] ^ {2} I [ Y > c (r - 2) ], \end{array}\tag{6.28}
$$

where $Y \sim \chi_{r-2}^{2}$ . An upper bound on (6.28) is obtained by dropping the indicator function, which gives 

$$
\begin{array}{l} r (\pi , \delta^ {R}) \leq r (\pi , \delta^ {\pi}) + \frac {1}{r - 2} \frac {\sigma^ {4}}{\sigma^ {2} + \tau^ {2}} E [ Y - c (r - 2) ] ^ {2} \\ \qquad = r (\pi , \delta^ {\pi}) + [ r + c (c - 2) (r - 2) ] \frac {\sigma^ {4}}{\sigma^ {2} + \tau^ {2}} \\ \qquad = r (\pi , \delta^ {c}). \end{array}\tag{6.29}
$$

This shows that $\delta^{R}$ has smaller Bayes risk than $\delta^{c}$ while remaining minimax. 

Since $E(Y-a)^{2}I(Y>a)$ is a decreasing function of a (Problem 6.14), the value c=2 minimizes (6.28) and therefore, among the estimators (6.25), determines the minimax estimator with minimum Bayes risk. However, for c=2, $\delta^{c}$ has the same (constant) risk as X, so we are trading optimal Bayes risk for minimal frequentist risk improvement over X, the constant risk minimax estimator. Thus, it may be better to choose c=1, which gives optimal frequentist risk performance and still provides good Bayes risk reduction over $\delta'$ . Table 6.1 shows the relative Bayes savings 

$$
r ^ {*} = \frac {r (\pi , \delta^ {c}) - r (\pi , \delta^ {\pi})}{r (\pi , \delta^ {c})}
$$

for c = 1. 


Table 6.1. Values of $r^*$ , the Relative Bayes Risk Savings of $\delta^R$ over $\delta^c$ , with $c = 1$


<table><tr><td>r</td><td>3</td><td>4</td><td>5</td><td>7</td><td>10</td><td>20</td></tr><tr><td><eq>r^{*}</eq></td><td>.801</td><td>.736</td><td>.699</td><td>.660</td><td>.629</td><td>.587</td></tr></table>

For other approaches to this “compromise” decision problem, see Bickel (1983, 1984), Kempthorne (1988a, 1988b), and DasGupta and Rubin (1988). 

Thus far, we have considered only continuous distributions, but the Stein effect continues to hold also in discrete families. Minimax proofs in discrete families have developed along two different lines. The first method, due to Clevenson and Zidek (1975), is illustrated by the following result. 

Theorem 6.8 Let $X_{i} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_{i})$ , $i = 1, \ldots, r$ , $r \geq 2$ , be independent, and let the loss be given by 

$$
L (\boldsymbol {\lambda}, \delta) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} (\lambda_ {i} - \delta_ {i}) ^ {2} / \lambda_ {i}.\tag{6.30}
$$

The estimator 

$$
\delta_ {c z} (\mathbf {x}) = \left(1 - \frac {c (\Sigma x _ {i})}{\Sigma x _ {i} + b}\right) \mathbf {x}\tag{6.31}
$$

is minimax if 

(i) $c(\cdot)$ is nondecreasing, 

(ii) $0 \leq c(\cdot) \leq 2(r - 1)$ , 

(iii) $b \geq r - 1.$ 

Recall (Corollary 2.20) that the usual minimax estimator here is X, with constant risk r. Note also that, in contrast to the normal-squared-error-loss case, by (ii) there exist positive values of c for which $\delta_{cz}$ is minimax provided $r \geq 2$ . 

Proof. If $Z = \Sigma X_{i}$ , the risk of $\delta_{cz}$ can be written as 

$$
\begin{array}{l} R (\boldsymbol {\lambda}, \delta_ {c z}) = E \left[ \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} \frac {1}{\lambda_ {i}} \left(\lambda_ {i} - X _ {i} + \frac {c (Z) X _ {i}}{Z + b}\right) ^ {2} \right] \\ = r + 2 E \left\{\frac {c (Z)}{Z + b} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} X _ {i} (\lambda_ {i} - X _ {i}) \right\} \\ + E \left\{\frac {c ^ {2} (Z)}{(Z + b) ^ {2}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} X _ {i} ^ {2} \right\}. \end{array}\tag{6.32}
$$

Let us first evaluate the expectations conditional on Z. The distribution of $X_{i}|Z$ is multinomial with $E(X_{i}|Z)=Z(\lambda_{i}/\Lambda)$ and $\mathrm{var}(X_{i}|Z)=Z(\lambda_{i}/\Lambda)(1-\lambda_{i}/\Lambda)$ , where $\Lambda=\Sigma\lambda_{i}$ . Hence, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} E \left[ \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} X _ {i} (\lambda_ {i} - X _ {i}) | Z \right] = \frac {Z}{\Lambda} [ \Lambda - (Z + r - 1) ] \\ E \left[ \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} X _ {i} ^ {2} | Z \right] = \frac {Z}{\Lambda} (Z + r - 1), \end{array}\tag{6.33}
$$

and, so, after some rearrangement of terms, 

$$
R (\boldsymbol {\lambda}, \delta_ {c z}) = r + E \left\{\frac {c (Z) Z}{\Lambda (Z + b)} \left[ 2 (\Lambda - Z) - 2 (r - 1) + c (Z) \frac {Z + r - 1}{Z + b} \right] \right\}.\tag{6.34}
$$

Now, if $b \geq r - 1, z + r - 1 < z + b$ , and $c(z) < 2(r - 1)$ , we have 

$$
- 2 (r - 1) + c (z) \frac {z + r - 1}{z + b} \leq - 2 (r - 1) + c (z) \leq 0,
$$

so the risk of $\delta_{cz}$ is bounded above by 

$$
R (\boldsymbol {\lambda}, \delta_ {c z}) \leq r + 2 E \left[ \left(\frac {c (Z) Z}{\Lambda (Z + b)}\right) (\Lambda - Z) \right].
$$

But this last expectation is the product of an increasing and a decreasing function of z; hence, by Lemma 6.6, 

$$
E \left(\frac {c (Z) Z}{\Lambda (Z + b)}\right) (\Lambda - Z) \leq E \frac {c (Z) Z}{\Lambda (Z + b)} E (\Lambda - z) = 0,\tag{6.35}
$$

[5.6] 

since $Z \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\Lambda)$ . Hence, $R(\lambda, \delta_{cz}) \leq r$ and $\delta_{cz}$ is minimax. 

If we recall Example 4.6.6 [in particular, Equation (4.6.29)], we see a similarity between $\delta_{cz}$ and the hierarchical Bayes estimators derived there. It is interesting to note that $\delta_{cz}$ is also a Bayes estimator (Clevenson and Zidek 1975; see Problem 6.15). 

The above method of proof, which relies on being able to evaluate the conditional distribution of $X_{i}|\Sigma X_{i}$ and the marginal distribution of $\sum X_{i}$ , works for other discrete families, in particular the negative binomial and the binomial (where $n$ is the parameter to be estimated). (See Problem 6.16.) However, there exists a more powerful method (similar to that of Stein's lemma) which is based on the following lemma due to Hudson (1978) and Hwang (1982a). The proof is left to Problem 6.17. 

## Lemma 6.9 Let $X_{i}, i = 1, \ldots, r$ , be independent with probabilities

$$
p _ {i} (x | \theta_ {i}) = c _ {i} (\theta_ {i}) h _ {i} (x) \theta_ {i} ^ {x}, \quad x = 0, 1, \ldots ,\tag{6.36}
$$

that is, $p_i(x|\theta_i)$ is in the exponential family. Then, for any real-valued function $g(\mathbf{x})$ with $E_{\theta}|g(\mathbf{X})| < \infty$ , and any number $m$ for which $g(\mathbf{x}) = 0$ when $x + i < m$ , 

$$
E _ {\theta} \theta_ {i} ^ {m} g (\mathbf {X}) = E _ {\theta} \left\{g (\mathbf {X} - m \mathbf {e} _ {i}) \frac {h _ {i} (X _ {i} - m)}{h _ {i} (X _ {i})} \right\}\tag{6.37}
$$

where $e_{i}$ is the unit vector with ith coordinate equal to 1 and the rest equal to 0. 

The principal application of Lemma 6.9 is to find an unbiased estimator of the risk of estimators of the form $\mathbf{X} + g(\mathbf{X})$ , analogous to that of Corollary 4.7.2. 

Theorem 6.10 Let $X_{1}, \ldots, X_{r}$ be independently distributed according to (6.36), and let $\delta^{0}(\mathbf{x}) = \{h_{i}(x_{i} - 1) / h_{i}(x_{i})\}$ [the estimator whose ith coordinate is $h_{i}(x_{i} - 1) / h_{i}(x_{i})$ ] be the UMVU estimator of $\theta$ . For the loss function 

$$
L _ {m} (\pmb {\theta}, \delta) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} \theta_ {i} ^ {m _ {i}} (\theta_ {i} - \delta_ {i}) ^ {2},\tag{6.38}
$$

where $\mathbf{m} = (m_1, \ldots, m_r)$ are known numbers, the risk of the estimator $\delta(\mathbf{x}) = \delta^0(\mathbf{x}) + g(\mathbf{x})$ is given by 

$$
R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) = R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta^ {0}) + E _ {\theta} \mathcal {D} (\mathbf {x})\tag{6.39}
$$

with 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {D} (\mathbf {x}) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} \left\{\frac {2 h _ {i} (x _ {i} - m _ {i} - 1)}{h _ {i} (x _ {i})} [ g _ {i} (\mathbf {x} - m _ {i} \mathbf {e} _ {i} - \mathbf {e} _ {i}) - g _ {i} (\mathbf {x} - m _ {i} \mathbf {e} _ {i}) ] \right. \\ \left. + \frac {h _ {i} (x _ {i} - m _ {i})}{h _ {i} (x _ {i})} g _ {i} ^ {2} (\mathbf {x} - m _ {i} \mathbf {e} _ {i}) \right\}. \end{array}\tag{6.40}
$$

Proof. Write 

$$
R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) = R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta^ {0}) - 2 E _ {\theta} \left\{\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} \theta_ {i} ^ {m} g _ {i} (\mathbf {X}) \left(\theta_ {i} - \frac {h _ {i} (X _ {i} - 1)}{h _ {i} (X _ {i})}\right) \right\}
$$

$$
+ E _ {\theta} \left\{\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} \theta_ {i} ^ {m} g _ {i} ^ {2} (\mathbf {X}) \right\}.
$$

and apply Lemma 6.9 (see Problem 6.17.) 

Hwang (1982a) established general conditions on $g(\mathbf{x})$ for which $\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{x}) \leq 0$ , leading to improved estimators of $\theta$ (see also Ghosh et al. 1983, Tsui 1979a, 1979b, and Hwang 1982b). We will only look at some examples. 

Example 6.11 Improved estimation for independent Poissons. The Clevenson-Zidek estimator (6.31) dominates $\mathbf{X}$ (and is minimax) for the loss $L_{-1}(\theta, \delta)$ of (6.38); however, Theorem 6.8 does not cover squared error loss, $L_0(\theta, \delta)$ . For this loss, if $X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i)$ , independent, the risk of an estimator $\delta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x} + g(\mathbf{x})$ is given by (6.39) with $\delta^0 = \mathbf{x}$ and 

$$
\mathcal {D} (\mathbf {x}) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} \left\{2 x _ {i} [ g _ {i} (\mathbf {x}) - g _ {i} (\mathbf {x} - \mathbf {e} _ {i}) ] + g _ {i} ^ {2} (\mathbf {x}) \right\}.\tag{6.41}
$$

The estimator with 

$$
g _ {i} (\mathbf {x}) = \frac {c (\mathbf {x}) k (x _ {i})}{\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r} k (x _ {j}) k (x _ {j} + 1)}, \quad k (x) = \sum_ {l = 1} ^ {x} \frac {1}{l},\tag{6.42}
$$

and $c(\mathbf{x})$ nondecreasing in each coordinate with 

$$
0 \leq c (\mathbf {x}) \leq 2 [ \# (x _ {i} ^ {\prime} s > 1) - 2 ]
$$

satisfies $\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{x}) \leq 0$ and hence dominates x under $L_{0}$ . (The notation $\#(a_{i}s > b)$ denotes the number of $a_{i}$ s that are greater than b.) 

For the loss function $L_{-1}(\pmb{\theta},\delta)$ , the situation is somewhat easier, and the estimator $\mathbf{x} + g(\mathbf{x})$ , with 

$$
g _ {i} (\mathbf {x}) = c (\mathbf {x} - \mathbf {e} _ {i}) \frac {x _ {i}}{\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r} x _ {i}},\tag{6.43}
$$

where $c(\cdot)$ is nondecreasing with $0 \leq c(\cdot) \leq 2(p - 1)$ , will satisfy $\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{x}) \leq 0$ and, hence, is minimax for $L_{-1}$ . Note that (6.43) includes the Clevenson-Zidek estimator as a special case. (See Problem 6.18.) 

As might be expected, these improved estimators, which shrink toward 0, perform best and give the greatest risk improvement, when the $\theta_{i}$ 's are close to zero and, more generally, when they are close together. Numerical studies (Clevenson and Zidek 1975, Tsui, 1979a, 1979b, Hudson and Tsui, 1981) quantify this improvement, which can be substantial. Other estimators, which shrink toward other targets in the parameter space, can optimize the region of greatest risk reduction (see, for example, Ghosh et al. 1983, Hudson 1985). 

Just as the minimaxity of Stein estimators carried over from the normal distribution to mixtures of normals, minimaxity carries over from the Poisson to mixtures of Poissons, for example, the negative binomial distribution (see Example 4.6.6). 

Example 6.12 Improved negative binomial estimation. For $X_{1}, \ldots, X_{r}$ independent negative binomial random variables with distribution 

$$
p _ {i} (x | \theta_ {i}) = \binom{t _ {i} + x - 1}{x} \theta_ {i} ^ {x} (1 - \theta_ {i}) ^ {t _ {i}}, \quad x = 0, 1, \ldots\tag{6.44}
$$

the UMVU estimator of $\theta_{i}$ is $\delta_{i}^{0}(x_{i}) = x_{i}/(x_{i} + t_{i} - 1)$ (where $\delta_{i}^{0}(0) = 0$ for $t_{i} = 1$ ). Using Theorem 6.10, this estimator can be improved. For example, for the loss $L_{-1}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \delta)$ of (6.38), the estimator $\delta_{0}(\mathbf{x}) + g(\mathbf{x})$ , with 

$$
g _ {i} (\mathbf {x}) = \frac {c (\mathbf {x} - \mathbf {e} _ {i}) x _ {i}}{\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {r} (x _ {j} ^ {2} + x _ {j})}\tag{6.45}
$$

and $c(\cdot)$ nondecreasing with $0 \leq c \leq 2(r - 2)/\min_{i}\{t_{i}\}$ , satisfies $\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{x}) \leq 0$ and, hence, has uniformly smaller risk than $\delta^{0}(\mathbf{x})$ . Similar results can be obtained for other loss functions (see Problem 6.19). Surprisingly, however, similar domination results do not hold for the MLE $\hat{\theta}_{i} = x_{i}/(x_{i} + t_{i})$ . Chow (1990) has shown that the MLE is admissible in all dimensions (see also Example 7.14). 

Finally, we turn to a situation where the Stein effect fails to yield improved estimators. 

Example 6.13 Multivariate binomial. For $X_{i} \sim b(\theta_{i}, n_{i})$ , $i = 1, \ldots, r$ , independent, that is, with distribution 

$$
p _ {i} (x | \theta_ {i}) = \binom {n _ {i}} {x} \theta_ {i} ^ {x} (1 - \theta_ {i}) ^ {n _ {i} - x}, \quad x = 0, 1, \ldots , n _ {i},\tag{6.46}
$$

it seems reasonable to expect that estimators of the form $\mathbf{x}+g(\mathbf{x})$ exist that dominate the UMVU estimator x. This expectation is partially based on the fact that (6.46) is a discrete exponential family. However, Johnson (1971) showed that such estimators do not exist in the binomial problem for squared error loss (see Example 7.23 and Problem 7.28). 

Theorem 6.14 If $k_{i}(\theta_{i})$ , $i = 1, \ldots, r$ , are continuous functions and $\delta_{i}(x_{i})$ is an admissible estimator of $k_{i}(\theta_{i})$ under squared error loss, then $(\delta_{1}(x_{1}), \ldots, \delta_{r}(x_{r}))$ is an admissible estimator of $(k_{1}(\theta_{1}), \ldots, k_{r}(\theta_{r}))$ under sum-of-squared-error loss. 

Thus, there is no “Stein effect” in the binomial problem. In particular, as $X_{i}$ is an admissible estimator of $\theta_{i}$ under squared error loss (Example 2.16), X is an admissible estimator of $\theta$ . 

It turns out that the absence of the Stein effect is not a property of the binomial distribution, but rather a result of the finiteness of the sample space (Gutmann 1982a; see also Brown 1981). See Note 9.7 for further discussion. 

## 7 Admissibility and Complete Classes

In Section 1.7, we defined the admissibility of an estimator which can be formally stated as follows. 

Definition 7.1 An estimator $\delta = \delta (\mathbf{X})$ of $\pmb{\theta}$ is admissible [with respect to the loss function $L(\pmb {\theta},\delta)$ ] if there exists no estimator $\delta^{\prime}$ that satisfies 

(7.1) 

(i) 

$$
R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta^ {\prime}) \leq R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) \quad \text { for   all } \boldsymbol {\theta},\tag{ii}
$$

$$
R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta^ {\prime}) <   R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) \quad \text { for   some } \boldsymbol {\theta},
$$

where $R(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \delta) = E_{\theta} L(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \delta)$ . If such an estimator $\delta'$ exists, then $\delta$ is inadmissible. When a pair of estimators $\delta$ and $\delta'$ satisfy (7.1), $\delta'$ is said to dominate $\delta$ . 

Although admissibility is a desirable property, it is a very weak requirement. This is illustrated by Example 2.23, where an admissible estimator was completely unreasonable since it used no information from the relevant distribution. Here is another example (from Makani 1977, who credits it to L.D. Brown). 

Example 7.2 Unreasonable admissible estimator. Let $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ be independent random variables, $X_{i}$ distributed as $N(\theta_i, 1)$ , and consider the estimation of $\theta_{1}$ with loss function $L((\theta_1, \theta_2), \delta) = (\theta_1 - \delta)^2$ . Then, $\delta = \text{sign}(X_2)$ is an admissible estimator of $\theta_{1}$ , although its distribution does not depend on $\theta_{1}$ . The result is established by showing that $\delta$ cannot be simultaneously beaten at $(\theta_1, \theta_2) = (1, \theta_2)$ and $(-1, \theta_2)$ . (See Problem 7.1.) 

Conversely, there exist inadmissible decision rules that perform quite well. 

Example 7.3 The positive-part Stein estimator. For $X \sim N_r(\theta, I)$ , the positive-part Stein estimator 

$$
\delta^ {+} (\mathbf {x}) = \left(1 - \frac {r - 2}{| \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}}\right) ^ {+} \mathbf {x}\tag{7.2}
$$

is a good estimator of $\theta$ under squared error loss, being both difficult to improve upon and difficult to dominate. However, as was pointed out by Baranchik (1964), it is not admissible. (This follows from Theorem 7.17, as $\delta^{+}$ is not smooth enough to be a generalized Bayes estimator.) Thus, there exists an estimator that uniformly dominates it. 

How much better can such a dominating estimator be? Efron and Morris (1973a, Section 5) show that $\delta^{+}$ is “close” to a Bayes rule (Problem 7.2). Brown (1988; see also Moore and Brook 1978) writing 

$$
\begin{array}{c} R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta^ {+}) = E _ {\theta} \left[ \frac {1}{r} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {r} (\theta_ {i} - \delta_ {i} (\mathbf {X})) ^ {2} \right] \\ = E _ {\theta} \mathcal {D} _ {\delta^ {+}} (\mathbf {X}), \end{array}\tag{7.3}
$$

where 

$$
\mathcal {D} _ {\delta^ {+}} (\mathbf {x}) = 1 + \frac {m ^ {2} (\mathbf {x}) | \mathbf {x} | ^ {2}}{r} - \frac {2}{r} \{(r - 2) m (\mathbf {x}) + 2 I [ m (\mathbf {x}) = 1 ] \}
$$

with $m(\mathbf{x}) = \min\{1, c(r - 2)/|x|^2\}$ (see Corollary 4.7.2), proves that no estimator $\delta$ exists for which $\mathcal{D}_{\delta}(\mathbf{x}) \leq \mathcal{D}_{\delta^{+}}(\mathbf{x})$ for all x. These observations imply that the inadmissible $\delta^{+}$ behaves similar to a Bayes rule and has a risk that is close to that of an admissible estimator. 

However, since admissibility generally is a desirable property, it is of interest to determine the totality of admissible estimators. 

Definition 7.4 A class of C of estimators is complete if for any $\delta$ not in C there exists an estimator $\delta'$ in C such that (7.1) holds; C is essentially complete if for any $\delta$ not in C there exists an estimator $\delta'$ in C such that (7.1)(i) holds. 

It follows from this definition that any estimator outside a complete class is inadmissible. If C is essentially complete, an estimator $\delta$ outside of C may be admissible, but there will then exist an estimator $\delta'$ in C with the same risk function. 

It is therefore reasonable, in the search for an optimal estimator, to restrict attention to a complete or essentially complete class. The following result provides two examples of such classes. 

## Lemma 7.5

(i) If $\mathcal{C}$ is the class of all (including randomized) estimators based on a sufficient statistic, then $\mathcal{C}$ is essentially complete. 

(ii) If the loss function $L(\theta, d)$ is convex in $d$ , then the class of nonrandomized estimators is complete. 

Proof. These results are immediate consequences of Theorem 1.6.1 and Corollary 1.7.9. $\square$ 

Although a complete class contains all admissible estimators, it may also contain many inadmissible ones. (This is, for example, the case for the two complete classes of Lemma 7.5.) A complete class is most useful if it is as small as possible. 

Definition 7.6 A complete class C of estimators is minimal complete if no proper subset of C is complete. 

Lemma 7.7 If a minimal complete class $\mathcal{C}$ exists, then it is exactly the class of all admissible estimators. 

Proof. It is clear that C contains all admissible rules, so we only need to prove that it cannot contain any inadmissible ones. Let $\delta \in C$ and suppose that $\delta$ is inadmissible. Then, there is a $\delta' \in C$ that dominates it, and, hence, the class $C \setminus \{\delta\}$ (C with the estimator $\delta$ removed) is a complete class. This contradicts the fact that C is minimal complete. □ 

Note that Lemma 7.7 requires the existence of a minimal complete class. The following example illustrates the possibility that a minimal complete class may not exist. (For another example, see Blackwell and Girshick 1954, Problem 5.2.1.) 

Example 7.8 Nonexistence of a minimal complete class. Let X be normally distributed as $N(\theta, 1)$ and consider the problem of estimating $\theta$ with loss function 

$$
L (\theta , d) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} d - \theta & \text { if } \theta <   d \\ 0 & \text { if } \theta \geq d. \end{array} \right.
$$

Then, if $\delta(x) \leq \delta'(x)$ for all $x$ , we have $R(\theta, \delta) \leq R(\theta, \delta')$ with strict inequality if $P_{\theta}[\delta(X) \leq \delta'(X)] > 0$ . 

Many complete classes exist in this situation. For example, if $\delta_{0}$ is any estimator of $\theta$ , then the class of all estimators with $\delta(x) < \delta_{0}(x)$ for some x is complete (Problem 7.4). We shall now show that there exists no minimal complete class. Suppose C is minimal complete and $\delta_{0}$ is any member of C. Then, some estimator $\delta_{1}$ dominating $\delta_{0}$ must also lie in C. If not, there would be no members of C left to dominate such estimators and C would not be complete. On the other hand, if $\delta_{1}$ dominates $\delta_{0}$ , and $\delta_{1}$ and $\delta_{0}$ are both in C, the class C is not minimal since $\delta_{0}$ could be removed without disturbing completeness. 

<!-- === Source: MinerU_markdown_Theory_of_Point_Estimation_401_2122709224994746379.md (Page 401) === -->

Despite this example, the minimal complete class typically coincides with the class of admissible estimators, and the search for a minimal complete class is therefore equivalent to the determination of all admissible estimators. The following results are concerned with these two related aspects, admissibility and completeness, and with the relation of both to Bayes estimators. 

Theorem 2.4 showed that any unique Bayes estimator is admissible. The following result replaces the uniqueness assumption by some other conditions. 

Theorem 7.9 For a possibly vector-valued parameter $\theta$ , suppose that $\delta^{\pi}$ is a Bayes estimator having finite Bayes risk with respect to a prior density $\pi$ which is positive for all $\theta$ , and that the risk function of every estimator $\delta$ is a continuous function of $\theta$ . Then, $\delta^{\pi}$ is admissible. 

Proof. If $\delta^{\pi}$ is not admissible, there exists an estimator $\delta$ such that 

$$
R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) \leq R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta^ {\pi}) \text {   for   all   } \boldsymbol {\theta}
$$

and 

$$
R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) <   R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta^ {\pi}) \text {   for   some   } \boldsymbol {\theta}.
$$

It then follows from the continuity of the risk functions that $R(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \delta) < R(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \delta^{\pi})$ for all $\theta$ in some open subset $\Omega_{0}$ of the parameter space and hence that 

$$
\int R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta) \pi (\boldsymbol {\theta}) d \boldsymbol {\theta} <   \int R (\boldsymbol {\theta}, \delta^ {\pi}) \pi (\boldsymbol {\theta}) d \boldsymbol {\theta},
$$

which contradicts the definition of $\delta^{\pi}$ . 

A basic assumption in this theorem is the continuity of all risk functions. The following example provides an important class of situations for which this assumptions holds. 

Example 7.10 Exponential families have continuous risks. Suppose that we let $p(x|\eta)$ be the exponential family of (5.2).
